arc_intro: FQ-142 starts here. Ravi Krishnan has flagged FoodQuick's IAM setup as priority one before next month's audit. First stop: figure out who actually has access to what — because right now, nobody can answer that question with confidence.

tasks.title: Priya cannot list S3 buckets

ticket.subject: Cannot list objects in fq-menu-assets — need S3 read
ticket.body:
Hi Cloud team,

I joined FoodQuick last week as a menu analyst. My IAM user is priya.sharma. I can sign in to the console, but when I open S3 I get AccessDenied listing fq-menu-assets.

Can you attach AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess to my user in the FoodQuick Prod account?

Account ID (from Ravi's onboarding mail): 482917364051
Region: ap-south-1

Thanks,
Priya

account_gate.hint: Priya pasted the Account ID in the ticket body — look for a 12-digit number.

tasks.explanation: Real IAM tickets start with Account ID, then the principal, then the exact permission change. You typed 482917364051, opened IAM → Users → priya.sharma, and attached AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess. That is the muscle memory FQ-142 needs before the audit.
tasks.ren_correct: Ticket resolved. You asked for Account ID, unlocked Prod, found priya.sharma, and attached AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess — not a quiz guess.
tasks.ren_wrong: Not done yet. Unlock the account from the ticket ID, open Users → priya.sharma, then Attach AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess.
hints: Account ID is in Priya's ticket body — type all 12 digits to open the console.
IAM → Users → search priya.sharma → Add permissions → AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess.

tasks.question: Before you touch anything else, Ravi wants to know: is FoodQuick's root account itself being used safely?
options: A) Root account should be used for daily admin work since it has full access
B) Root account should be used only once during initial setup, then locked away with MFA enabled
C) Root account is only a risk if it's shared, individual use is always fine
D) Root account doesn't need MFA if the password is long enough
tasks.explanation: The root account is the master key. Use it only for initial setup, enable MFA, then lock it away. Day-to-day work belongs on IAM users and roles.
tasks.ren_correct: Correct! Root locked away — non-negotiable for the rest of this investigation.
tasks.ren_wrong: Not quite. Daily root use is always a risk. Setup only, then lock it.

tasks.scenario: You pull up the full current IAM state to map exactly how bad this is before touching anything.
tasks.broken_config:
Current IAM Setup:
├── Root Account
│   ├── MFA: DISABLED
│   ├── Access Keys: 2 ACTIVE
│   └── Last used: 3 days ago
│
├── IAM Users
│   ├── dev-shared (used by 10 developers)
│   │   └── Policy: AdministratorAccess
│   └── backup-script
│       └── Policy: AdministratorAccess
│
└── No Groups configured
what_to_find: Root account used daily — should be locked away after setup
Root account MFA disabled — critical vulnerability
Root account has active access keys — must be deleted
10 developers sharing one IAM user — zero individual audit trail
backup-script has AdministratorAccess — needs only S3/RDS read
No IAM groups — impossible to manage permissions at scale
tasks.correct_fix:
Correct target structure:
├── Root Account — MFA enabled, keys deleted, setup-only
├── IAM Groups — Developers (scoped), DevOps (scoped)
├── IAM Users — one per person, assigned to correct group
└── IAM Role — backup-role, scoped to only what the script needs
tasks.explanation: Seven problems on one map — that is the full FQ-142 scope. Map everything before you fix anything, or you will miss something.

tasks.question: Before executing anything, plan the fix in the correct order. Arrange these steps.
items: Secure the root account first (MFA + delete access keys)
Create proper IAM groups matching actual roles (Developers, DevOps)
Create individual IAM users for each of the 10 developers
Assign each new user to their correct group
Migrate backup-script from AdministratorAccess to a scoped role
Only after all of the above — deactivate dev-shared
tasks.explanation: Secure root first so you keep control. Only deactivate dev-shared after every person has a working individual login — otherwise you lock out the team.

tasks.scenario: You start executing the plan. First: root account. You enable MFA using an authenticator app and confirm the setup with two consecutive codes. Next, you check for active access keys on root.
tasks.question: You find 2 active access keys on the root account, both unused in the last 90 days according to Access Advisor. What do you do?
options: A) Leave them — they might be needed for something later
B) Delete both immediately — root should never have active access keys, used or not
C) Deactivate but don't delete, in case they're needed
D) Rotate them to new keys instead of deleting
tasks.explanation: Root access keys should not exist at all — used or unused. Delete them. Deactivating or rotating still leaves a standing risk.
tasks.ren_correct: Correct! Root access keys should not exist at all, period.
tasks.ren_wrong: Not quite — do not just deactivate or rotate. Root access keys are not needed; delete them.

tasks.scenario: Root is secured. Now you're creating the 10 individual developer accounts and assigning them to a new 'Developers' group. Midway through, priya-dev messages you: 'Wait — before you deactivate dev-shared, one thing. Ravi mentioned last week that a contractor, external to the company, was ALSO using dev-shared for a two-week project that ended a month ago.'
tasks.question: How does this change your plan?
expected_answer_contains: This is more urgent than a routine cleanup — an external, non-employee had access via a shared account with no individual tracking
Check CloudTrail for what that contractor actually did during and after their access period, since there's no way to filter by 'contractor' specifically without knowing the exact dates
This reinforces why dev-shared needs to be deactivated as soon as possible, not just cleaned up later
tasks.explanation: A former contractor also used the shared login — that makes this urgent. You cannot filter CloudTrail by 'contractor', so use the project date window, and deactivate the shared account as soon as individual users are ready.

tasks.scenario: Following priya-dev's tip, you pull CloudTrail for the dev-shared user around the contractor's project window and slightly after. Something looks off — one entry, after the contractor's project officially ended, that nobody on the team seems to remember.
tasks.diagnosis: This event happened 12 days AFTER the contractor's project ended, at 2:41 AM, from an IP address nobody on the current team recognizes. Someone — possibly the former contractor, possibly someone else who obtained the shared credentials — generated a brand new access key for dev-shared well after they should have lost access entirely. This cannot be fully explained yet with what you know right now.
tasks.fix: This cannot be resolved in this task alone. Document it precisely (timestamp, IP, event type) and flag it for deeper investigation — this is now officially 'something to watch' rather than something you can close today. Proceed with securing the rest of the account, but this thread stays open.
tasks.explanation: Document the unexplained CreateAccessKey event precisely (time, IP, event type) and keep the thread open. You cannot close it from this task alone.

tasks.scenario: Setting the mystery aside for now, you finish executing the plan: 10 individual users created, all assigned to Developers group, backup-script migrated to a scoped role, dev-shared finally deactivated. Do a final check before calling this piece done.
tasks.broken_config:
Post-Fix IAM Setup:
├── Root Account — MFA ✓, no access keys ✓
├── IAM Groups
│   └── Developers (10 members) — Policy: AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess, AmazonEC2ReadOnlyAccess
├── IAM Users
│   ├── priya.dev, karthik.dev, + 8 others → Developers group ✓
│   └── dev-shared — STATUS: still shows 'Active' in the console
└── IAM Role: backup-role — S3:GetObject, RDS:CreateDBSnapshot ✓
what_to_find: dev-shared user still shows as Active — deactivation did not actually complete despite the plan saying it should be done
This is the exact kind of gap that undermines an otherwise correct cleanup — one leftover thread
tasks.correct_fix: Go back and actually disable dev-shared's console access and deactivate any access keys still attached to it — including, notably, the mysterious one created 12 days after the contractor's project ended (from T7). Confirm status shows fully deactivated before considering this closed.
tasks.explanation: The cleanup looks almost done, but dev-shared is still Active — including that mysterious key. Finish full deactivation before you call the piece closed.

tasks.scenario: dev-shared is now fully deactivated. Ravi asks: 'Good — but how do we make sure we never end up back here? What's the actual process going forward, for both new employees AND future contractors?'
options: A) Just remember to be careful next time — no formal process needed

B) Every new person (employee or contractor) gets their own IAM user in the correct group. Contractors get a documented END DATE at creation time, with a calendar reminder to deactivate on that exact date — not 'whenever someone notices.'
C) Only employees need individual accounts, contractors can keep sharing one since they're temporary anyway
D) Require all contractors to use their personal AWS accounts instead of FoodQuick's account entirely
tasks.explanation: Everyone gets an individual account in the right group. Contractors also get a documented end date and a calendar reminder — 'someone will remember' is not a process.
tasks.ren_correct: Correct — this is the long-term fix: process, not just cleanup.
tasks.ren_wrong: Not quite. 'Be careful next time' is not a process. Contractors need an end date plus a reminder.

tasks.scenario: Time to report back to Ravi and close this piece of FQ-142.
tasks.question: Write your status update. It should cover: what you fixed, what's now in place going forward, and the one thing that's still genuinely unresolved.
expected_answer_contains: Root account secured with MFA, no access keys
10 individual developer accounts created, properly grouped, dev-shared fully deactivated
New process in place for future contractors with defined end dates

Flag clearly: an unexplained access key was created on dev-shared 12 days after a former contractor's project ended, from an unrecognized IP — this needs further investigation and should not be considered closed
tasks.explanation: Report what you fixed, what process is now in place, and clearly flag the unexplained post-project access key as still open.

arc_outro: Identity Layer: secured. But something doesn't add up — a key created weeks after access should have ended, from nowhere anyone recognizes. Ravi says: 'Good work. Keep that CloudTrail entry in mind — I have a feeling we haven't seen the last of it.' Next: FoodQuick's services are still using old habits that are just as risky as shared logins ever were.
